chapters.title: Leningrad
paragraphs: Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin was born on October 7, 1952, in Leningrad, now St. Petersburg. His parents had survived the Second World War. Two older brothers died before he was born. The family lived in a communal apartment, in a city still getting over the German siege.

As a boy he took up sambo, and later judo. Both became part of how the public saw him. He studied law at Leningrad State University and graduated in 1975. One teacher, Anatoly Sobchak, would later bring him into city government.

chapters.title: The KGB, and the family
paragraphs: After university he joined the KGB, the Soviet security and intelligence service. The service posted him to Dresden, in East Germany, in 1985. He was still there when the Berlin Wall fell in 1989. He returned to Leningrad in 1990 and left the KGB in 1991.

He married Lyudmila Shkrebneva, a former flight attendant, in 1983. They had two daughters, Maria and Katerina. In 2013 they said publicly that they were separating, and the divorce was finalized in 2014. U.S. Treasury sanctions in 2022 identified the adult daughters as Maria Vorontsova and Katerina Tikhonova.

chapters.title: City hall, then the Kremlin
paragraphs: He worked for Sobchak in St. Petersburg, overseeing foreign economic relations, and rose to first deputy head of the city government. After Sobchak lost the 1996 mayoral election, Putin moved to Moscow and took a post in Boris Yeltsin’s presidential administration.

Yeltsin put him in charge of the Federal Security Service, the FSB, in 1998, and made him prime minister in August 1999. Fighting in Dagestan, and deadly apartment bombings, came before Russia’s second war in Chechnya. Putin’s hard response raised his standing across the country. Yeltsin resigned on December 31, and Putin became acting president. He won the March 2000 election with about 53 percent of the vote.

chapters.title: The recovery, and a tighter grip
paragraphs: The economy recovered after Russia’s 1998 financial crisis. Higher energy prices, a cheaper ruble, and policy changes all played a part. The government built reserves out of oil revenue, and household incomes came back. After the turmoil of the 1990s, that improvement did a lot to secure his support.

The Kremlin took a firmer hold on television and on the regions. In 2001, state-controlled Gazprom took over the independent broadcaster NTV. Oil tycoon Mikhail Khodorkovsky was arrested in 2003 and later imprisoned. After more than 300 people died in the Beslan school siege in 2004, Putin moved to replace direct elections for governors with presidential nominations.

He won a second term in 2004. At the Munich Security Conference in 2007 he attacked American dominance of the post-Cold War order and criticized NATO’s enlargement. The speech marked a turn, after the cooperation that had followed the September 11 attacks.

chapters.title: Four years as prime minister
paragraphs: The constitution barred a third presidential term in a row. Dmitry Medvedev became president in 2008 and appointed Putin prime minister. Putin kept substantial influence through those four years. The presidential term was lengthened from four years to six, for people taking office later.

In August 2008, a long escalation over South Ossetia became a war between Russia and Georgia. Russia then recognized South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent. Georgia, and most other countries, still regard both as Georgian territory.
A disputed parliamentary election in December 2011 drew large protests. Putin won the presidency again in March 2012 and began his third term that May.

chapters.title: Crimea, Syria, and the 2016 election
paragraphs: Weeks after Russia hosted the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi, Russian forces took control of Crimea and Moscow annexed the peninsula. The UN General Assembly affirmed Ukraine’s territorial integrity and said the referendum used to justify the change had no validity. Fighting also broke out in eastern Ukraine, between Kyiv’s forces and separatists backed by Russia.

In 2015 Russia intervened militarily in Syria, on the side of Bashar al-Assad’s government. That help kept Assad in power for nearly another decade. He fled to Russia after his government collapsed in December 2024.

The 2019 report from U.S. Special Counsel Robert Mueller documented Russian interference in the 2016 American election: social-media influence operations, and the theft and release of political emails. The investigation did not establish that the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in that interference.

chapters.title: Rewriting the term limits
paragraphs: He began a fourth term in 2018. A package of constitutional changes in 2020 created a two-term limit, but it left the incumbent’s earlier terms out of the count. He could therefore run in 2024, and possibly again in 2030, which is a legal route to staying in office until 2036.

There was less and less room for opposition politics. Anti-corruption campaigner Alexei Navalny survived a nerve-agent poisoning in 2020. Russian authorities arrested him when he returned from treatment in Germany in January 2021, and a court later outlawed his organizations as extremist.

chapters.title: The invasion of Ukraine
paragraphs: On February 24, 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Putin said it was necessary for Russian security. The UN General Assembly condemned the invasion as aggression and demanded that Russia withdraw. It later rejected Russia’s claims to annex four more Ukrainian regions.

Western governments imposed sanctions, and more of Russia’s trade shifted toward China. At home, the authorities restricted independent reporting and used new laws against anti-war speech. In June 2023, Wagner leader Yevgeny Prigozhin led a short armed mutiny. It ended before his forces reached Moscow.

The crackdown was not limited to anti-war politics. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated what the authorities called the “international LGBT movement” as extremist. UN experts warned that the decision put LGBTQ people, and the groups supporting them, at risk of prosecution.

chapters.title: The warrant, and the inquiries
paragraphs: In March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and for Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights. The allegation is the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. The warrants are pretrial decisions. Russia does not accept the court’s jurisdiction.

A British public inquiry concluded in 2016 that Putin probably approved the 2006 operation that killed former Russian security officer Alexander Litvinenko in London. Another British inquiry concluded in 2025 that he had authorized the 2018 operation to poison Sergei and Yulia Skripal. Dawn Sturgess, a British civilian, died after she was exposed to the poison.

Navalny died in a penal colony in February 2024. Russian authorities attributed the death to natural causes. In February 2026, five European governments said laboratory evidence indicated that poisoning was highly likely to have caused it.

chapters.title: A fifth term, still at war
paragraphs: He began a fifth presidential term in May 2024. The election commission reported that he won 87.28 percent of the vote. Russia did not invite observers from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe. Opposition campaigning and independent media were severely restricted.

By November 2026 the independent paper Novaya Gazeta said it was closing its Moscow office after thirty years. Staff cited official pressure. The paper had already faced limits on publishing, and it had been designated a foreign agent.

He met Donald Trump in Alaska in August 2025. They did not announce a ceasefire. After another round of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi that November, Putin met the American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow on November 12. They reached an agreement in principle on a prisoner exchange. The wider war continued.
